flashcard_questions.q: Which literary movement did Wordsworth belong to?
Which oxymoron describes the boy's feelings as he takes the boat?
flashcard_questions.a: “an act of stealth and troubled pleasure”

flashcard_questions.q: Which simile describes the boat's movement across the lake?
Which term means an experience of awe and terror before something vast in nature?
What does the repetition of ‘huge’ in the mountain's description emphasise?
flashcard_questions.a: The overwhelming size of the mountain.

flashcard_questions.q: Which phrase personifies the mountain as acting with a will of its own?
Which verb shows the mountain chasing the boy across the water?
Which phrase completes the mountain's personification as a creature?
How does the boy row back to shore once the mountain appears?
Where does the volta fall in The Prelude extract?
flashcard_questions.a: At the moment the mountain rises into view.

flashcard_questions.q: What happened to Wordsworth's thinking for many days after the encounter?
flashcard_questions.a: His brain “worked with a dim and undetermined sense of unknown modes of being”.

flashcard_questions.q: Which quotation shows nature haunting the boy even in sleep?
flashcard_questions.a: “Huge and mighty forms… were a trouble to my dreams.”

flashcard_questions.q: What effect does the repeated ‘no’ create in the lines about familiar shapes?
flashcard_questions.a: It strips away the pleasant natural world the boy once enjoyed.

flashcard_questions.q: Which verse form is The Prelude extract written in?
Why does Wordsworth write The Prelude in the first person?
flashcard_questions.a: It makes the experience personal and draws the reader into his psychological journey.

notes: 15 cards: 7 theme-to-quotation, 4 quotation-to-technique or effect, 2 structure and form (blank verse, first-person narration), 1 definition-front term card (the sublime), 1 volta-placement card. Broke the 'huge peak, black and huge' line into a repetition card plus a personification card, because quoting the line whole trips the enumeration rule. Dropped the anthology-comparison paragraph: two poems fit each link, so no card would be self-gradable.
